entries.title: Angels get the best of Sox rookie starter Noah Schultz
entries.summary: <p>ANAHEIM, Calif. – It wasn’t the best of outings for Sox left-hander Noah Schultz on Wednesday. He walked the first batter he faced, but worked out of the first inning unscathed.</p><p>The proverbial roof then caved in during a five-run second that included a three-run Travis d’Arnaud homer as Schultz took his second defeat of the season in an 8-2 loss to the Angels at Angel Stadium. That closed a six-game Sox western road trip at 3-3.</p><p>Schultz allowed seven runs on seven hits with four walks and two strikeouts before Sox manager Will Venable yanked him with two out in the fourth.</p><p>“Today it was just a case where they hit some tough pitches,” Venable said. “The homer was a well-located fastball. Four walks. You have to be a lot more aggressive in the zone. It was just one of those days when he got burned on some pitches.”</p><p>The outing was the antithesis of Schultz’s last one. He opened the roadie this past Friday with oddly an 8-2 win over the Padres at Petco Park in San Diego during which he allowed no runs on two hits in six innings. The walks still plagued him in that game. He had three, two of them in the first inning but pitched out of trouble in that one.</p><p>No such luck against the Angels on Wednesday. What can he learn from it?</p><p>“There’s a lot of stuff,” he said. “I can definitely look at some video. Make sure I wasn’t giving away any pitches, that I wasn’t getting repetitive. I thought I was going hard, soft, hard, soft pretty frequently. I’ll just have to talk to our staff and make some changes for next week.”</p><p>It was definitely the worst game pitched by a starter on this trip. In the first five games the other four starters had only allowed six earned runs. Schultz blew that up.</p><p>He’s not going to be perfect all the time, it was noted.</p><p>“Yeah, for sure,” Venable said. “I really like where he’s at. He’ll continue to build on all of these starts. This obviously wasn’t the best one. But he’ll continue to go to work and he’ll be fine.”</p><p><b>It’s May and what’s up with Kyle Teel?</b></p><p>The projected starting catcher has been down with a Grade 2 right hamstring strain since March 10 running out a double for Team Italy in a victory over Team USA during the World Baseball Classic. Though he’s been throwing and hitting and even crouching to do some catching, running has been problematic Teel admitted on Wednesday.</p><p>“Every day I’m taking a step to be back playing baseball,” Teel said. “The rehab is going good. I’m running better every single day. And it’s only a matter of time before I’ll be ready to go on my rehab assignment and be back.”</p><p>Teel has been saying this for weeks. But the reality is this: Around April 19, Teel had a setback running and his rehab assignment at that point was delayed. Originally he was only supposed to be out four-to-six weeks. That timetable has long since come and gone.</p><p>You can’t play if you can’t run and the Sox continue to delay his minor-league rehab assignment. Plus, Venable has been satisfied with the work of Drew Romo both behind the plate and working with the pitching staff.</p><p>“Teel is getting closer,” Venable said. “I feel really good about his progress, him getting up to speed with his running. But some of the recovery has been slower than we wanted. We’ll continue to push him to run the bases when we go home and see where we are at.”</p><p></p><table class="cf wS" role="presentation" style="border-collapse: collapse;" id="rte-18c04dc0-49aa-11f1-a5fd-a97fdcf92862"><tbody><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amq" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px 16px; vertical-align: top; width: 44px; visibility: hidden;"></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1" class="amr" style="margin: 0px; padding: 0px; width: 648px;"><br></td></tr></tbody></table><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p><p></p>

entries.title: CTU threatens to sue CPS over unpaid stipends for dozens of athletic directors
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Teachers Union is threatening to file a lawsuit against Chicago Public Schools over what the union’s lawyers say is the delayed payment of some $300,000 in stipends for high school athletic directors.</p><p>On Monday an attorney representing the union sent the district a letter saying “to avoid a lawsuit” CPS should distribute the $7,525 stipends to athletic directors at 41 high schools who haven’t been paid for their work during the fall athletic season. The union’s lawyer gave the district a deadline of Thursday.</p><p>Illinois law requires wages to be paid no later than 13 days after the pay period in which they are earned, and “we are now months past that deadline,” attorney Josiah Groff wrote. The fall sports season typically ends by December. Prior to this school year, Groff wrote, athletic directors typically got paid within two months of their season ending.</p><p>According to the letter, the district also hasn’t paid stipends for nearly 70 athletic directors for the winter season, which concluded at the end of March. The union said it would take legal action if those aren’t paid soon, too.</p><p>A spokesperson for CPS said the district is reviewing the claims made in the letter and that about half of the athletic directors mentioned are scheduled to receive their payment on May 15, though it was unclear what season that work was for.</p><p>“The others have either already received payment or do not meet the eligibility requirements for the stipend at this time,” the spokesperson said in a statement. “The District is focused on processing these payments and is addressing the issue through the appropriate labor-management channels.”</p><p>The district has been dealing with ongoing financial troubles. CPS is projected to end the school year with a $45 million deficit and may have to contend with a $529 million deficit next year. <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/04/10/cps-archdiocese-funding-catholic-school-special-education-tutoring" target="_blank" ><u>Recently, CPS was caught up in a disagreement with the Archdiocese of Chicago</u></a> over whether the district was holding back federal funding meant for students with disabilities who attend private schools.</p><p>In the letter, Groff attributed the stipend delay to an “internal disagreement within CPS” about whether the pay should come from the district’s centralized budget or individual school budgets.</p><p>Wendy Weingarten, the sports committee liaison for the CTU, said every athletic director should be getting the stipend and that should come from the district’s central budget. Weingarten and some athletic directors say CPS officials have recently told the union that athletic directors at large high schools aren’t eligible for the stipend.</p><p>According to the CTU’s lawyer, the 41 high schools where athletic directors have not been paid are some of the district’s largest, including Lane Tech, Whitney Young, Amundsen, Jones and Curie.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.ctulocal1.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/CBA-24-2026-03-20.pdf" target="_blank" ><u>According to the latest agreement</u></a> between CPS and CTU, the district is responsible for funding a full-time athletic director for large and extra large high schools, in addition to setting aside at least $3 million per year to use for stipends for part-time athletic directors and elementary school athletic liaisons, which are like athletic directors for earlier grades.</p><p>“If the board is providing that $3 million, I don't know why small and medium schools” have to use their own budgets to pay, Weingarten said.</p><p>The contract also states that the $7,525 athletic director stipends are intended for high schools without a full-time athletic director position.</p><p>Emily Crawford, who is the full-time athletic director at Chicago Academy High School, is among those who haven’t gotten their stipend for the fall season. She’s responsible for many tasks, such as scheduling buses to games, coordinating payments for tournaments, uniforms and equipment and tracking athlete eligibility.</p><p>Crawford doesn't have an assistant, so she's responsible for coordinating the school’s 300 athletes by herself. “We’re on the smaller end of large,” Crawford said. The stipend helps compensate for the extra hours she puts in, she said.</p><p>“I think last week I didn’t leave the school multiple days until 8 p.m.," Crawford said.</p><p>She thinks all athletic directors should get a stipend, and the idea that only smaller schools get one is backwards.</p><p>“The larger schools are doing substantially more work than a school that only has eight athletic programs. We have more students, more athletes, more coaches, more staff doing more work,” Crawford said. “I think it is really invalidating and disheartening that work is not being valued.”</p>

entries.title: Eaglet hatches in Chicago for the first time in more than 100 years
entries.summary: <p>For the first time in more than a century, an eaglet has hatched within Chicago's city limits.</p><p>The baby bird hatched at a nest at Park 597, also known as SEPA Station #1, near the Calumet River on the border of Hegewisch and South Deering, according to the Chicago Park District.</p><p>While several of the birds have attempted to nest and hatch in the city, April 28 was the first time an eaglet reared its head, according to the park district. Officials and local birding groups documented nesting behavior starting in February.</p><p>In recent years, work has been done to restore the 10.3-acre woodland, including removing and controlling invasive plants, seeding native species and installing native herbaceous plant life.</p><p>But the city is discouraging the public from visiting the nest site because human presence can negatively impact the wildlife.</p><p>“Restoring park habitats to their natural state maximizes positive impact, making experiences like this one truly powerful,” said Chicago Park District General Superintendent and CEO Carlos Ramirez-Rosa in a statement. “We’d like it to be a regular occurrence, and for that to happen, we need the public’s cooperation to see even more wildlife thrive in our urban parks.”</p><p>But there are still ways for people to get involved with the city’s newest residents — the park district is holding a naming contest.</p><p>Up to three options for the eaglet's name <a class="Link" href="https://bit.ly/NameTheEaglet2026" target="_blank" ><u>can be submitted</u></a> per person by May 15; local birding groups and the Park District Natural Resources team will narrow them down to three choices May 19 before the winner is picked in a final public vote.</p>

entries.title: Obama Presidential Center sells out first month hours after tickets become available
entries.summary: <p>Just hours after <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/things-to-do/2026/04/30/obama-presidential-center-museum-tickets-go-on-sale-may-6-heres-what-to-know" target="_blank" ><u>going on sale</u></a> Wednesday morning, tickets for the Obama Center sold out for the first month, with more flying off the digital shelves as the day went on.</p><p>New Jersey-born Lake View resident Andres Chamorro said it still wasn’t as bad as trying to secure entry to local shows for big artists, such as Chappell Roan.</p><p>“I’d say this was less stressful than trying to get Geese tickets,” Chamorro said. “It was painful to lose out on opening weekend, but I was up against a good part of the city, if not the state.”</p><p>The Obama Presidential Center didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment or to provide figures on how many tickets were sold Wednesday.</p><p>The museum debuts June 18 with an invitation-only grand opening ceremony, then opens to the public the next day — Juneteenth. Donors were offered early access to tickets last month, however, so those looking to get in on opening day faced an uphill battle from the start.</p><p>Chamorro had intended to get opening weekend tickets for him and his boyfriend, but it had sold out by the time he got through the queue.</p><p>“I’ve seen how the area has been changed and revitalized over the years, and we’ve been watching the obelisk rise up,” Chamorro said. “So to see the culmination on opening day would've been cool.”</p><p>All of June and half of July have already sold out, though the calendar largely remains open into November. In October and November, that includes all Tuesdays, which are free days for Illinois residents.</p><p>Tickets cost $30, though there's a $4 discount for Illinois residents, a $3 discount for out-of-state kids and $11 off for in-state kids. Tickets can’t be returned, transferred or sold.</p><p>Chamorro plans to get tickets eventually, and suggests others try to land a weekday to make the whole process easier, even if the initial ticket rush seems to be over. He said he might try to avoid packed weekends or times when schools are likely to bringi students.</p><p>“For something like this, it’s something I want to take all of it at once,” he said.</p>

entries.title: UChicago Medicine raising awareness about stroke risk
entries.summary: <p>Lucas Wittwer was bouldering at a climbing gym when he fell and passed out.</p><p>It was 2022. He was only 27 years old, and when he regained consciousness he felt fine.</p><p>“I was very annoyed that they were not letting me just go,” Wittwer said recently. “I felt fine. I was slightly confused.”</p><p>He was taken to Mount Sinai Hospital and later to the University of Chicago Medical Center, where he was treated for a hemorrhagic stroke from an aneurysm. He still has no memory of two of those days, during which doctors performed an aneurysm embolization.</p><p>Wittwer joined the University of Chicago Medical Center and Philips, a health technology company, on Wednesday on a behind-the-scenes day held as part of National Stroke Awareness Month. Over the last two decades, the risk of a stroke has increased by 50%, according to the World Health Organization. Former Mayor Richard M. Daley, Chicago’s longest-serving mayor, was hospitalized recently after his third stroke.</p><p>Some patients, like Wittwer, had no warning signs before an aneurysm. But doctors at the University of Chicago Medical Center said balance abnormality, eyesight changes, facial droop or difficulty speaking all could be signs of a stroke.</p><p>They also usually see a link between a stroke and existing conditions, in particular hypertension. Cedric McKoy, a nurse practitioner for the hospital’s stroke program, said that’s one reason he urges people to focus on getting their high blood pressure under control and improving their diet to reduce the risk.</p><p>While the number of strokes across the country has fluctuated, McKoy said he continues to see a rise in stroke patients among the patients — predominately people of color — they serve on the South Side .</p><p>Another reason for more stroke patients is improved treatments like reperfusion therapy, which helps restore blood flow after a heart attack, said Dr. James Siegler, medical director of the hospital’s Comprehensive Stroke Center.</p><p>“We’re restoring healthy brain function, getting patients mobilized, but they still have those underlying vascular risk factors, and they’ve had those vascular risk factors build up over time,” Siegler said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a He was speaking Wednesday at a look behind the scenes at the UChicago Medicine Center for Care and Discovery in Hyde Park.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Giacomo Cain/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The technology doctors use to treat stroke patients has also vastly improved even in the last couple of years, said Dr. Tareq Kass-Hout, a stroke neurologist who treated Wittwer. The hospital is also using a room known as an intervention suite to bypass the emergency room for certain patients who rate higher on a stroke scale.</p><p>The room has a machine that rotates around a person to scan them, allowing doctors to immediately start a procedure rather than waiting for a CT scan and moving the patient around the hospital, Kass-Hout said. Doctors say they consider every second critical when treating a stroke patient.</p><p>The procedure usually involves using tiny wires and catheters inserted through a person’s wrist or groin to extract a blood clot or repair an aneurysm.</p><p>It’s considered a less invasive procedure and sometimes can take as little as six minutes. Kass-Hout said he thinks technology, including artificial intelligence, will continue to improve so much he could one day conduct these types of procedures remotely, providing wider access to patients who live in more rural areas.</p><p>“I always joke with my kids that they sit on their phone playing FIFA, one day I’m going to be sitting playing stroke. They’re doing their thing, I’m doing my thing at the same time,” Kass-Hout said. “This is, again, not science fiction. We’re going to see it in the next few years.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-3b0000"
